item.content:encoded:
There were 13 outfield-eligible players worth at least $20 in the FanGraphs Player Rater in 2026, just two fewer than the first base spot. If you remember that you only need to start one first baseman (and potentially a corner infielder and DH) while you might need to start as many as five outfielders at a time, well, you can see why this is problematic.
That's not to say the outfield is somehow a wasteland for Fantasy right now. First base was unusually strong in 2026, but in 2025, there were three times as many $20 players with outfield eligibility as at first base. And it's worth noting that the 13 $20 outfielders in 2026 are actually a few more than 2025's nine.
On the whole, I look at outfield as a position with a decent amount of depth in a three-outfielder, 12-team league. You should be able to draft a full lineup without feeling too bad about your outfield options in that formula.
Once you start getting into five-outfielder leagues, and especially deeper leagues with 15 teams, it starts to feel a lot more thin. That's to be expected, of course, but it's important to keep that in mind when you're preparing for the 2027 season. You don't have to make the position a priority in every draft, but if you aren't cognizant of it, you could end up with a real weakness in those deeper leagues.
For more on the state of the outfield position, .
2026 Outfield Review
- Pete Crow-Armstrong, CHC: .280 - 119 - 45 - 107 - 41
- Yordan Alvarez, HOU: .316 - 105 - 42 - 106 - 1
- Fernando Tatis Jr., SDP: .289 - 96 - 25 - 83 - 38
- Randy Arozarena, SEA: .281 - 113 - 26 - 79 - 26
- Jordan Walker, STL: .269 - 97 - 29 - 102 - 22
- James Wood, WSN: .265 - 106 - 30 - 77 - 21
- Jackson Chourio, MIL: .291 - 96 - 25 - 75 - 23
- Alec Burleson, STL: .279 - 89 - 26 - 116 - 4
- Jake McCarthy, COL: .291 - 80 - 15 - 83 - 32
- Michael Harris II, ATL: .294 - 79 - 26 - 87 - 12
- Jackson Merrill, SDP: .254 - 86 - 26 - 87 - 27
- Bryce Harper, PHI: .269 - 93 - 29 - 87 - 7
- Jake Bauers, MIL: .266 - 93 - 26 - 86 - 11
- Seiya Suzuki, CHC: .270 - 96 - 26 - 86 - 3
- Carson Benge, NYM: .282 - 86 - 20 - 65 - 22
- Andy Pages, LAD: .274 - 75 - 23 - 85 - 13
- Corbin Carroll, ARI: .239 - 91 - 22 - 78 - 21
- Oneil Cruz, PIT: .280 - 65 - 20 - 67 - 30
- Daylen Lile, WSN: .246 - 81 - 22 - 89 - 15
- Jac Caglianone, KCR: .289 - 72 - 23 - 75 - 7
- Bryan Reynolds, PIT: .261 - 102 - 17 - 72 - 9
- Chandler Simpson, TBR: .306 - 66 - 0 - 38 - 46
- Riley Greene, DET: .280 - 79 - 21 - 75 - 3
- Ceddanne Rafaela, BOS: .285 - 67 - 16 - 70 - 17
"Marginal player signs with the Rockies and has a Coors Field-inflated career season" used to be a pretty reliable archetype. Still, the Rockies have given Fantasy players little to get excited about in recent years. Jake McCarthy stands out as a notable exception, as his contact-and-speed profile proved to be a perfect fit for Coos Field. We're talking about relatively easy career-best production across the board, in a way that feels relatively obvious in retrospect. I don't have a ton of faith that this would prove replicable in any other ballpark — the gap between his .321 expected wOBA and his .349 actual mark was the 20th biggest in baseball — but it works there. As long as he isn't traded, McCarthy is a good bet to replicate his 2026 success.
I also want to highlight Harris and Merrill, because it feels very natural to group them together. They're both younger than you might realize – Harris will turn 26 shortly before his sixth MLB season in March, while Merrill won't even be 24 on Opening Day. They're also both linked by the combination of plus athleticism and bat speed, plus pretty poor approaches at the plate. They are, on the whole, capable of overcoming their poor swing decisions with outlier outcomes when they make contact, but that isn't always the case for either. Hence, the lengthy slumps that have held both back in recent years. They both got the good end of their range of outcomes in 2026, and we saw how high the ceiling can be for both. But drafting either for their 2026 outcome will carry inherent risks until they show some growth in their plate discipline.
Biggest Breakout from 2026
Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs
How could it be anyone else? Crow-Armstrong went from being a talented but deeply flawed hitter to arguably the best player in baseball, and he did it in-season. Early on, he looked more or less like the same guy he had always been, walking just nine times in 128 plate appearances through the end of June; he walked at least 12 times in each of the final five months of the season, something he had never done in any of his previous 13 months. He did that without sacrificing the pull-side power that has long been a key part of his game, and it turned him into one of the most dominant hitters in the game. Expecting all of those gains to carry over into 2027 might be asking a bit much — sometimes guys just get super locked in for a while — but he's clearly a much-improved hitter, and one who should be the first player taken in every single Roto league in 2027. And he shouldn't go much later in points leagues, where he was also the top player in 2026.
Honorable Mention: Jordan Walker, Cardinals
Okay, so if it were going to be anyone but Crow-Armstrong, it would be Walker, who went from being one of the biggest prospect busts in recent seasons to one of the best players in Fantasy. Walker still had pretty bad plate discipline and swing-and-miss issues, but he overcame that by being more aggressive early in the count and by doing more damage when he did make contact. The plate discipline issues and a late-season swoon — his expected wOBA dropped from .374 to .290 from the first half to the second — hint at the kind of risk involved in buying fully into what he did in 2026, and I suspect I'll be a little lower on him than the consensus. On the other hand, those were the exact reasons I cited to avoid Crow-Armstrong before the season, and look how that turned out. There's something to be said for just betting on the young, super-talented players when they show it.
Biggest Bust from 2026
The overall numbers don't show it, but Judge looked more or less like himself before he started dealing with that rib injury. In March and April, he posted a .450 xwOBA, right in line with his typical mark, but then things went downhill even before he ultimately went on the IL with a fractured rib. Was his downturn because of the injury? If so, then I think you can still make the case for him as a top-five pick in any league. But we're talking about a guy who will be 35 early next season, coming off a largely lost season that also came with an apparent decline in the underlying skill level, and that's a lot of red flags to overlook in a top-five pick. I might end up with Judge ranked that way come the spring, but it won't feel good.
Honorable Mention: Kyle Tucker, Dodgers
Maybe you don't think he was worth the contract the Dodgers gave him. Fair enough; you won't be alone in holding that opinion. But anyone who tells you there was any way to see this kind of disaster coming from Tucker is just lying to you. A 29-year-old went out and posted the worst batting average, on-base percentage, and slugging percentage of his career, and in two of those cases, it wasn't even close. Tucker had the combination of bat speed, athleticism, and plate discipline that should protect him against this kind of drop-off. Maybe the lights in L.A. were too bright for him. Maybe the pressure of the contract got to him. But I don't believe Tucker has just completely lost the ability to be an impact player, and he's still in what should be one of the best lineups in baseball, so I'll buy the bounce-back at what should be a steeply discounted price. The fact that he put together an excellent September and a very good postseason run certainly makes that an easier story to tell, of course.
Biggest rankings movers from 2026 to 2027
Up: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs; Yordan Alvarez, Astros; Jordan Walker, Cardinals; Jake Bauers, Brewers
As maybe the biggest Yordan Alvarez believer in the entire Fantasy industry coming into 2026, I do worry there's going to be a big overcorrection on him in 2027. We didn't learn anything new about Alvarez. If you think 2026 was a breakout season of some sort for him, I'm sorry, but you just weren't paying attention; he's just always been this good. His .442 xwOBA was higher than his career average, sure, but it was also not even the highest of his career, and he had a separate season with a .436 mark, too. The skills have always been there, but the difference is that he stayed healthy in 2026 after a bunch of injuries in previous seasons. I'm thrilled that he stayed healthy, and the fact that he did it in a season when his standing among Fantasy players was never lower is a good reminder that the Fantasy community isn't nearly as good at predicting who will and won't stay healthy as we think. But that will also be true in 2027: He'll be a top-five pick in most leagues despite the injury risk not being substantially different than it was last season. That's not to say he shouldn't be a top-five pick, of course; it's to say that he should have been a lot closer to a top-five pick last season than he was.
You could make a case for Bauers as the biggest breakout at outfield, because he was viewed as an even bigger afterthought than Walker was. He was a 30-year-old platoon specialist, after all! That he somehow went out in 2026 and put up a .901 OPS against lefties and had the best season of his career by a mile came completely out of nowhere, and it's going to be very interesting to see what the market for him as a free agent looks like this offseason. I buy a lot of what he did in 2026, and I suspect there will be enough skepticism around it to keep his price pretty reasonable. But betting on age-30 breakouts is historically a pretty bad idea, so you'll have to get a pretty big discount on what he did in 2026 to make him worth the risk, I think.
Down: Ronald Acuna, Braves; Kyle Tucker, Dodgers; Wyatt Langford, Rangers; Brent Rooker, Athletics
I wanted to make Langford one of the biggest bust picks, if only to highlight the fact that he has almost certainly been the least profitable pick in Fantasy over the past three years. He has struggled to stay healthy and just hasn't been the impact player you'd expect from a guy who had the kind of prospect pedigree he did — not to mention the benefit of the doubt the Fantasy community has continued to give him. I suspect that will come to an end in 2027, and … it kind of makes me more excited about buying into him this season. Because, for as frustrating and disappointing as he's been as a big-leaguer, his per-162 game pace for his career is pretty terrific: 90 runs, 24 homers, 24 steals, and 77 RBI. If he just does that in 2027, isn't that worth something like a fifth-round pick? And I don't think that's the ceiling for Langford, who has put up those numbers at a very young age while playing through a variety of injuries and has certainly flashed a higher ceiling at times. I'm not trying to excuse his poor performance; I'm just pointing out that all he has to do is stay healthy to be a very good Fantasy option. That's usually a good player to buy into at a discount.
The notoriously frugal A's are surely feeling some degree of buyer's remorse on Rooker's contract, but that contract should assure that he continues to play every day for them. His disappointing season came to an end after just 48 games, but he was on pace for another 30-homer season despite the injury. The .200 average is a tough look, as was the career-worst 32% strikeout rate, and the big drop off as a 31-year-old will rightly lead to plenty of skepticism around the potential of a bounce back. But that will also mean Rooker will come at a huge discount, potentially with a price outside the top 200 in many drafts. I'll buy that dip, personally. If you can buy him as a very cheap bench bat, there's no downside.
Offseason preview
Who needs an upgrade most?
A bunch of these teams are straddling the line between trying to go for it and needing to rebuild. The Reds could very well be in the market for a big upgrade in the outfield, or they could decide to move Elly De La Cruz and hit the reset button (again). The Astros could decide to give it one more run with this core, or they could move Alvarez and pivot to the future. The Phillies seem most likely to try to take a big swing, if only because Dave Dombrowski only knows how to take big swings. However, the Cardinals loom as a team that is ascending and could decide to get involved in the free-agent market with their core of cost-controlled position players.
Top impending free agents
- Randy Arozarena
- Seiya Suzuki
- Ian Happ
- Jake Bauers
- Trent Grisham
- Daulton Varsho
- Luis Robert
- Ramon Laureano
- George Springer
Arozarena is such a fascinating free agent. He's coming off a perfectly timed career-best season, but he'll be 32 before Opening Day and has rated out as a pretty terrible defender for several years running. There's probably no chance he gets anything more than a five-year contract in free agency, and he might need to agree to a move to DH as soon as 2027, two things that might be a tough pill to swallow. But having the best season of his career in the toughest offensive environment in baseball is no small thing, and nobody can deny his flair for the dramatic would be a great fit for a team with championship aspirations. The underlying skill set doesn't look so different from previous seasons, but his price will likely be higher than ever, making him one of the more obvious players to avoid in drafts for 2027, no matter where he lands.
Suzuki and, to a lesser extent, Happ look like players who will carry pretty solid value in Fantasy no matter where they land, but everyone else looks pretty context-dependent. Varsho's pull-heavy swing (and elite center field defense) would be a perfect fit for the Yankees, for example, but would be a much less interesting profile elsewhere. Stay tuned.
Trade candidates 
- Yordan Alvarez, Astros
- Jarren Duran, Red Sox
- Steven Kwan, Guardians
- Byron Buxton, Twins
- Brent Rooker, Athletics
- Jake McCarthy, Rockies
Alvarez feels like the biggest wild card here. The Astros won the AL West, but with just a .500 record, and they had such a poor showing in a two-game Wild Card round loss to the White Sox that the hometown crowd showered them with boos along the way. The Astros have lost their long-held edge over the competition, and while Alvarez's contract isn't expiring, he only has two years left on a relatively below-market deal. So this might be their last chance to maximize their return for him. The Astros are in flux in a lot of ways after firing Dana Brown, so they might not be positioned to make a big, franchise-altering move, but they would probably be best served trying to get off the treadmill of mediocrity sooner rather than later.
It increasingly looks like the Red Sox should have traded Duran at least a year ago, if not longer. All of a sudden, he's a 30-year-old corner outfielder who probably shouldn't play every day against lefties, and while he'll likely still earn a below-market salary in arbitration, he no longer looks like a real bargain. His skill set still has plenty of value for Fantasy (20 homers, 21 steals will always play), and I'd bet on him improving on last year's .207 average, but this isn't an early-round profile anymore.
Top rookies to know for 2026
- Josue De Paula, Dodgers
- Walker Jenkins, Twins
- Eduardo Quintero, Dodgers
- Theo Gillen, Rays
- Mike Sirota, Dodgers
- Zyhir Hope, Tigers
- Edward Florentino, Pirates
- Eric Hartman, Braves
- Drew Burress, Athletics
- Josiah Hartshorn, Cubs
- Lazaro Montes, Mariners
Jenkins is probably the most likely player here to be in an Opening Day lineup – I'm not sure what would have to happen for him not to be there, absent injury. He didn't take the league by storm in his first 26 games, but he was actually pretty great once he got adjusted, hitting .385/.400/.615 with just three strikeouts over his final 10 games. He has power, speed, and an excellent approach at the plate and should be a popular breakout candidate for 2027.
But not as popular as De Paula could be. I say "could" because, well, there's no obvious place for him to play. It's definitely not going to be in right field or DH, and slotting De Paula in at left field would require finding somewhere for Teoscar Hernandez and his large salary to go. Center field is the biggest hole in the Yankees outfield, but De Paula hasn't played there since 2023, and … well, you see the problem here. De Paula destroyed Double-A and very much passed the eye test in 11 MLB games, earning not-totally-unfair comparisons to Juan Soto and Yordan Alvarez for his approach at the plate. He could be an absolute star, but given the roster crunch and the fact that he's only 21 and hasn't played at Triple-A yet, this might be a situation like Junior Caminero's a few years back – remember, he debuted toward the end of the 2023 season but wasn't an everyday player until August of 2024. I hope it doesn't take that long, but we'll have to at least consider the possibility that it will.
item.category: Yankees vs Red Sox Wild Card

item.title: [NBC Sports] 2027 Fantasy Baseball Mock Draft: Can you trust Garrett Crochet in 2027? What about Byron Buxton?

item.content:encoded:
The 2026 MLB Postseason is entering the Championship Series, but the time for fantasy baseball analysis never truly stops. Last Monday, we started our Rotoworld Staff and Friends Fantasy Baseball Mock Draft for the 2027 season. While many places do a “too early” mock draft, we’d argue that it’s not really too early to look ahead to next season. I’ve been posting a collection of “look back” articles reviewing the best picks of the 2026 season, the worst picks, and my key lessons, but all of these articles are linked together by the idea that immediately taking stock in the season, before the offseason hype starts to creep in, can be an incredibly valuable experience.
So we invited our staff and a few of our friends to put together a 15-round mock draft that we’ll complete over the next couple of weeks and continue to break down for you in chunks over on our site. Today you’ll get the first four rounds, and then I’ll be back to update the next four or five rounds by the end of the week and then do one more update at the end.
We hope you find it a useful tool, and we’ll see how much it changes over the next few weeks.
2027 Fantasy Baseball Mock Draft
| Round 1 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 1 | RotoPat (Rotoworld) | Shohei Ohtani | UT/SP | LAD |
| 2 | George Bissell (Rotoworld) | Pete Crow-Armstrong | OF | CHC |
| 3 | Frank Stampfl (CBS Sports) | Bobby Witt Jr. | SS | KC |
| 4 | D.J. Short (Rotoworld) | Elly De La Cruz | SS | CIN |
| 5 | Scott Pianowski (Yahoo Sports) | Fernando Tatis Jr. | 2B/OF | SD |
| 6 | Rivers McCown (Rotoworld) | Junior Caminero | 3B | TB |
| 7 | Matthew Pouliot (Rotoworld) | Aaron Judge | OF | NYY |
| 8 | Dave Shovein (Rotoworld) | Juan Soto | OF | NYM |
| 9 | Frank Ammirante (RotoBaller) | Jackson Chourio | OF | MIL |
| 10 | James Schiano (Rotoworld) | James Wood | OF | WSH |
| 11 | Justin Mason (FanGraphs) | Yordan Alvarez | OF | HOU |
| 12 | Jorge Montanez (Rotoworld) | Ben Rice | 1B | NYY |
Perhaps the story here is that no starting pitchers went in the first 12 picks. One season after Tarik Skubal, Garrett Crochet, and Paul Skenes either got hurt or had down seasons, none of the drafters seemed willing to roll the dice on a starting pitcher with their first pick. Honestly, I can’t blame them. Early-round hitters, on average, continue to out-produce early-round pitchers at similar draft costs. The pitchers that do hit can make a huge difference for your team, but the risk is exponentially higher. A hitter taken here who fails to produce value, like Kyle Tucker this year, can still produce $10 of value, but a pitcher who goes in the first round and fails to produce value is almost always due to injury, and they can give you no value.
We did see Pat still choose Shohei Ohtani (dual position eligible here) as the top pick over Pete Crow-Armstrong. There are certainly some questions as to whether or not Ohtani’s body can hold up to a whole season as a starting pitcher and a DH, which will bring some uncertainty to his fantasy value. We also know he’s clearly not healthy right now, so we’ll need to see if any of these injuries require offseason surgery, but PCA has certainly worked his way into the conversation to be first overall.
A big surprise for some might be seeing Fernando Tatis Jr. this high. The Padres outfielder was one of the best hitters in baseball from June 1st on after a batting stance change allowed him to clear his hips more easily and unlock the pull-side power that we know he has. He also picked up 2B eligibility this season, which will be huge for him at a pretty barren position.
Jackson Chourio and James Wood have used breakout seasons to propel them into the first-round conversation, and you have to wonder if there is yet another level of development there, and Yordan Alvarez now has outfield eligibility in all formats, which makes him an even safer pick here. There look to be plenty of outfield options in the first round, including injured New York stars Juan Soto and Aaron Judge. Both of them being in the first round makes sense, but we may start to have to ask real questions about Judge’s durability. He’ll be 35 years old next season. He’s a giant human being, and the strain of playing the outfield every day at that size takes a real toll on your body. The fact that his two major injuries this season were both soft tissue or muscle injuries (and not a broken toe) should begin to raise some questions about whether or not we can count on 150+ games from Judge going forward.
His teammate, Ben Rice, used a 40-home run season to catapult him into the first round as well. That’s without catcher eligibility. Rice was the first 1B off the board in this draft, and I really find it hard to argue against that. Some guys in the next round have an argument, but Rice is a tremendous overall hitter. He has clear power. He plays in a great park for his approach, and there is no way the Yankees are going back to regularly sitting him against lefties. Even if Rice is more of a mid-30s home run hitter going forward than a true 40+ guy, his approach at the plate makes me feel good about his contact and batting average, and that puts him ahead of the guys who will follow him in round two.
| Round 2 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 13 | Jorge Montanez | CJ Abrams | SS/2B | WSH |
| 14 | Justin Mason | Jose Ramirez | 3B | CLE |
| 15 | James Schiano | Jacob Misiorowski | SP | MIL |
| 16 | Frank Ammirante | Tarik Skubal | SP | LAD |
| 17 | Dave Shovein | Ronald Acuña Jr. | OF | ATL |
| 18 | Matthew Pouliot | Nick Kurtz | 1B | OAK |
| 19 | Rivers McCown | Jordan Walker | OF | STL |
| 20 | Scott Pianowski | Kyle Schwarber | DH | PHI |
| 21 | D.J. Short | Pete Alonso | 1B | BAL |
| 22 | Frank Stampfl | Corbin Carroll | OF | ARI |
| 23 | George Bissell | Cam Schlittler | SP | NYY |
| 24 | Roto Pat | Yoshinobu Yamamoto | SP | LAD |
And now the pitchers start to come off the board. Not really a surprise with who the first three arms were off the board: Jacob Misiorowski, Tarik Skubal, and Cam Schlittler. I assume those will be the top three arms in pretty much all rankings heading into 2027. Pat did snag Yoshinobu Yamamoto as the fourth starter picked in this round, and while some may argue for Chris Sale or Cristopher Sanchez here, there’s a strong case that Yamamoto could be locked into the fourth spot. There is still some elevated risk with starting pitchers in the second round, but at least every one of these teams added an elite bat in the first round, and both George and Pat were able to take second elite bats at the start of the third round, so this risk feels more palatable.
CJ Abrams is another player, like Tatis Jr., who picked up second base eligibility in most formats. That’s huge for his fantasy value. So is hitting .261 with 33 home runs and 34 steals while driving in 106 runs. Abrams will be 26 years old next season, and while his future in Washington is a bit cloudy, he’s an elite offensive talent who is finally making good on that promise.
We had some former first-round picks fall into the second with Jose Ramirez, Ronald Acuña Jr., and Corbin Carroll all falling into the second round. The falls make sense too. Ramirez and Acuña Jr. now just have a bit more injury risk than some of the other players going in the first round. Ramirez still has great upside at a position that lacks talent, which may drive his price up, but he’ll be 34 years old, and he hit just 12 home runs and batted .235 this year after hamate surgery. Are you willing to bet that he gets back to 100% of his old self, or do we think it’s more likely that he’ll be 75-80% of the guy who almost went 40/40 in 2024? Acuña Jr. is a harder bet because he has now played under 108 games in three straight seasons and has played over 120 games once since 2019. It’s hard to bet on a full season of production, and with PCA, Chourio, and James Wood emerging, it makes sense to go with the younger/healthier players.
At the same position, the most interesting name in this round is probably Jordan Walker. He had a breakout season this year, hitting .269 with 29 home runs, 102 RBI, and 22 steals. He also just turned 24 years old, so there is plenty of growth still possible for him. He struggled through an injury at the end of the year, which hurt his September stats, but there will be no half measures with Walker in 2027. You have to either be all-in on the fact that 2026 was a real breakout for a former top prospect or just acknowledge that you won’t be getting him in your drafts.
Pete Alonso and Nick Kurtz are the two first basemen I alluded to earlier who land here in round 2. Kurtz played just 99 games this season due to injury but still hit 21 home runs while batting .256. We know the hitting environment in Sacramento is elite, so he should still be going in this range.
| Round 3 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 25 | Roto Pat | Sal Stewart | 1B | CIN |
| 26 | George Bissell | Konnor Griffin | SS | PIT |
| 27 | Frank Stampfl | Miguel Vargas | 3B | CHW |
| 28 | D.J. Short | Cristopher Sanchez | SP | PHI |
| 29 | Scott Pianowski | Paul Skenes | SP | PIT |
| 30 | Rivers McCown | Mason Miller | RP | SD |
| 31 | Matthew Pouliot | Julio Rodriguez | OF | SEA |
| 32 | Dave Shovein | Trea Turner | SS | PHI |
| 33 | Frank Ammirante | Gunnar Henderson | SS | BAL |
| 34 | James Schiano | Jackson Merrill | OF | SD |
| 35 | Justin Mason | Kevin McGonigle | SS/3B | DET |
| 36 | Jorge Montanez | Jesus Luzardo | SP | PHI |
We see three current-year rookies go in Round 3, announcing themselves as top-tier talents for years to come, and it’s hard to argue against it. Sal Stewart, Konnor Griffin, and Kevin McGonigle all showed that they can handle this level of competition, and we should expect more growth from these young players. The same goes for Miguel Vargas, who is not a rookie but broke out in 2026 in a way that suggests consistent value. He’s always had an elite plate approach, and now he added pull-side power to that equation. Vargas will be 27 years old and is in an ascending lineup, so he belongs in this range.
We saw the next group of starting pitchers go with Cristopher Sanchez, Paul Skenes, and Jesus Luzardo. Obviously, the name everybody will want to talk about is Skenes. It was a bad year for the Pirates ace, and while he claimed he wasn’t hurt, his velocity fell throughout the year, and he was not missing as many bats. There had been some previous concerns that his fastball wasn’t a huge whiff pitch to righties (10.7% swinging strike rate in 2025), but Skenes saw huge strides there this season. However, that was basically the only place he got better, and by elevating his four-seamer more for whiffs, he also started to allow more hard contact. It’s hard to see Skenes being this bad again, but we also can’t ignore how this season went.
Mason Miller went here as the first closer off the board, and three former first-round picks fell in Gunnar Henderson, Trea Turner, and Julio Rodriguez. I covered Gunnar and Trea in my article on what I learned from the 2026 fantasy baseball season, so you should read that, but essentially their 2025 price baked in a full return to peak value and ignored the warning signs from that season. We don’t appear to be doing that this year.
| Round 4 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 37 | Jorge Montanez | Drew Rasmussen | SP | TB |
| 38 | Justin Mason | Chris Sale | SP | ATL |
| 39 | James Schiano | Francisco Lindor | SS | NYM |
| 40 | Frank Ammirante | Kyle Tucker | OF | LAD |
| 41 | Dave Shovein | Brice Turang | 2B | MIL |
| 42 | Matthew Pouliot | Zach Neto | SS | LAA |
| 43 | Rivers McCown | Oneil Cruz | OF | PIT |
| 44 | Scott Pianowski | Matt Olson | 1B | ATL |
| 45 | D.J. Short | Carson Benge | OF | NYM |
| 46 | Frank Stampfl | Chase Burns | SP | CIN |
| 47 | George Bissell | Hunter Goodman | C | COL |
| 48 | Roto Pat | Nolan McLean | SP | NYM |
Now we answer the question of how far Kyle Tucker falls as Frank Ammirante takes him with the fourth pick in the fourth round, 40th overall. I covered Tucker more extensively in my article revisiting the top two rounds of 2025 drafts, but the miss on Tucker was essentially looking at pedigree (his seasons before his last two injured ones) and also the team context (a move to the Dodgers) and ignoring that he hadn’t had a fully productive year in a while. I’m not sure anybody expected that Tucker would see his barrel-rate collapse and that he would make uncharacteristically aggressive, out-of-character swing decisions, so perhaps we can expect a slight bounce back to his previously healthy form.
Four more starting pitchers go off the board here, and it’s an interesting group. Drew Rasmussen was brilliant this season, but it was also his first over 150 innings, and he’s had three elbow surgeries. Can you bank on his health as your ace? Kind of the same question for Chris Sale, who will be 38 next year and has basically alternated healthy years with injured years. After being hurt for basically all of 2021-23, he threw 178 innings in 2024, then 125 in 2025, and then 163 this year. What’s in store for 2027?
The final two arms were young pitchers in Chase Burns and Nolan McLean. The Burns pick makes sense given his elite strikeout upside and plus raw stuff, but McLean is harder to see here. Not that he’s a bad pitcher, but taking him as the 11th starting pitcher is assuming tons of growth. His 26% strikeout rate and 16.6% K-BB% don’t line up with some of the elite arms in this range, and his 10.5% swinging strike rate continues to suggest some concern with his ability to consistently miss bats. He’ll be 26 next year, and he’s clearly a talented arm, but taking him this high means he really HAS to take the next step, or he won’t return value.
Oneil Cruz’s bounce-back season pushed him up into the fourth round, and he’s joined by young outfielder Carson Benge, who hit .282 with 20 home runs and 22 steals in his rookie season. He didn’t get the fanfare of the other rookies who went higher in this draft, but Benge has a true five-category skill set and should be in an improved lineup next season.
We also saw our first catcher go off the board in Hunter Goodman. Keep in mind that this is a one-catcher format, which is why you’re not seeing a lot of catchers go early, but George wanted to lock up an elite bat at the position. With Ben Rice no longer catcher eligible, Goodman was the top fantasy catcher this season after hitting 41 home runs, driving in 88 runs, and hitting .245 in Coors Field. There’s little reason to believe he can’t do it again.
| Round 5 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 49 | Roto Pat | Rafael Devers | 1B | SF |
| 50 | George Bissell | Cade Smith | RP | CLE |
| 51 | Frank Stampfl | Zack Wheeler | SP | PHI |
| 52 | D.J. Short | Parker Messick | SP | CLE |
| 53 | Scott Pianowski | Randy Arozarena | OF | SEA |
| 54 | Rivers McCown | Dylan Cease | SP | TOR |
| 55 | Matthew Pouliot | Vladimir Guerrero Jr. | 1B | TOR |
| 56 | Dave Shovein | Logan Gilbert | SP | SEA |
| 57 | Frank Ammirante | Garrett Crochet | SP | BOS |
| 58 | James Schiano | Bryce Harper | 1B/OF | PHI |
| 59 | Justin Mason | Logan Henderson | SP | MIL |
| 60 | Jorge Montanez | Michael Harris II | OF | ATL |
A few big-name starting pitchers with major injuries go in this round. Zack Wheeler (SP12) missed half of this past season after having thoracic outlet surgery, Garrett Crochet (SP16) missed basically the whole season with a shoulder injury, Dylan Cease (SP14) ended the season on the injured list with a shoulder injury, and Logan Henderson (SP17) has missed time in each of the last two seasons with injuries. We’re now outside of the top 10 starting pitchers, so these guys don’t HAVE to be your ace, but this is still an early round draft pick for pitchers who have some overall health concerns. I understand the argument for their upside, and while I may not make the pick here, that’s just my personal drafting philosophy.
Parker Messick (SP13) and Logan Gilbert (SP15) also go in this round. Both of them feel a bit safer from a health standpoint, and there is still an argument that Gilbert has another level of production to hit. I have him as a top-10 starting pitcher, so I like him going as the 15th starter off the board.
We see Cade Smith go here as the second closer off the board, and Rafael Devers and Bryce Harper make sense in this range as veteran 1B who are likely past their peak but continue to produce overall solid numbers. Devers really turned things around after a slow start to the year and seems as consistent as ever.
We also see two outfielders coming off big seasons in Michael Harris II and Randy Arozarena. James Schiano and I actually discussed this exact either-or in a video we recorded after the Braves were eliminated from the postseason. I picked Harris II easily because I believe in the changes he’s made over the last year-and-a-half, and I’m not looking to pay for Arozarena’s career year.
Lastly, we need to address Vladimir Guerrero Jr., who finally goes off the board here in the fifth. We all know how Vlad Jr. struggled this year, but he’s now going as the sixth 1B, late in the fifth round, which is way more palatable for me. I know the power wasn’t there, but we have enough of a track record to feel confident that he is at least a 20-25 home run bat who can hit .280 in what should be a solid lineup. That’s still a solid fantasy asset; it’s just not a pick to make in the first three rounds of your draft. Also, getting corrective eye surgery can’t be bad either.
| Round 6 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 61 | Jorge Montanez | Jac Caglianone | OF | KC |
| 62 | Justin Mason | Jhoan Duran | RP | PHI |
| 63 | James Schiano | Jazz Chisholm Jr. | OF | NYY |
| 64 | Frank Ammirante | Cal Raleigh | C | SEA |
| 65 | Dave Shovein | Andres Munoz | RP | SEA |
| 66 | Matthew Pouliot | Bryan Woo | SP | SEA |
| 67 | Rivers McCown | Drake Baldwin | C | ATL |
| 68 | Scott Pianowski | Alex Bregman | 3B | CHC |
| 69 | D.J. Short | Gavin Williams | SP | CLE |
| 70 | Frank Stampfl | Shea Langeliers | C | OAK |
| 71 | George Bissell | Kade Anderson | SP | SEA |
| 72 | Roto Pat | Wyatt Langford | OF | TEX |
This is a super interesting round to me, and I can’t make much sense of it, haha. There seem to be no runs here or any real trend.
We do get more catchers off the board here with Cal Raleigh, Drake Baldwin, and Shea Langeliers. It feels a little early to be in a one-catcher format, but everybody has their own strategy. Baldwin feels like a great pick after his 2026 season, and while I do think Raleigh is going to bounce back after a down 2026 season, I’m not sure he’d be the gamble I take this early in the sixth round. Yes, you might be getting 30+ home runs from that spot, but the batting average will be a drain, and we have no idea if that lineup will be any good.
Jhoan Duran goes off the board as the third closer, and then Andres Munoz next was a bit of a surprise. He wasn’t really in a closer committee in Seattle this year; they just didn’t get a lot of saves. His SIERA and underlying metrics look a lot better than his ERA, so it does feel like he was just unlucky, but I’m not that convinced the Mariners will be that good next year, and Munoz has never delivered as a consistent top 5-8 closer.
Three risky hitters with plenty of upside also go in this round: Jac Caglianone, Jazz Chisholm Jr., and Wyatt Langford. We don’t really know where Jazz will be next year, but it seems like it won’t be New York. That’s likely a big park downgrade for him. His batting average also regressed pretty drastically this season, which had been a concern for him in previous years. We know the speed will always be there, so he’ll need to land in a park where the power can come as well, but this feels like a fair spot for him. Caglianone is also a popular breakout pick because his batted ball data has been really strong. I like the idea of him taking a big step next season, but a top-60 pick does feel like you’re paying as if the breakthrough is a given. We all know the deal with Langford at this point too. A top-70 pick on him feels right if he can stay healthy, but can he ever stay healthy?
Bryan Woo at SP18 and Gavin Williams at SP19 feel like strong picks at this point. Both of them have immense strikeout upside and the ability to be top-10 starting pitchers. Woo had a bad stretch this season but seemed to right the ship at the end of the year, and Williams still seems to have one iffy inning every game where his command gets wonky. However, the big surprise here was Kade Anderson. I know he was an elite pitching prospect, but he doesn’t have elite MLB velocity or Stuff+, which means that he gets by with command and a deep enough pitch mix. I think he will be a solid starting pitcher, but I’m not sure I see the ceiling to take him as SP20, especially in what will be his rookie season.
| Round 7 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 73 | Roto Pat | Henry Bolte | OF | OAK |
| 74 | George Bissell | Riley Greene | OF | DET |
| 75 | Frank Stampfl | Andy Pages | OF | LAD |
| 76 | D.J. Short | William Contreras | C | MIL |
| 77 | Scott Pianowski | Ceddanne Rafaela | OF | BOS |
| 78 | Rivers McCown | Byron Buxton | OF | MIN |
| 79 | Matthew Pouliot | Ketel Marte | 2B | ARI |
| 80 | Dave Shovein | Max Fried | SP | NYY |
| 81 | Frank Ammirante | Manny Machado | 3B | SD |
| 82 | James Schiano | Payton Tolle | SP | BOS |
| 83 | Justin Mason | Seiya Suzuki | OF | CHC |
| 84 | Jorge Montanez | Josh Hader | RP | HOU |
Round 7 gave us quite the run on outfielders. After Wyatt Langford ended last round, Henry Bolte, Riley Greene, Andy Pages, Ceddanne Rafaela, Byron Buxton, and Seiya Suzuki all came off the board in the seventh round. Bolte is the name that probably stands out. The Athletics’ rookie hit .277/.359/.405 in 119 big league games with 11 home runs and 21 steals. In 65 games in the second half, Bolte hit .289/.370/.448 with eight of his home runs and a 9.2% barrel rate. Bolte has always had loud raw tools, but he has struggled to lift the ball consistently, which has limited his power output. We started to see that a little more from him in the second half and, if it carries over, he has the makings of a 20/30 hitter in a great ballpark. Pat taking him at 73 means Bolte kind of HAS to get close to that in order to return value, which makes the pick a bit of a risk but not one without some logic to it.
The Buxton and Suzuki picks have their own risk too, along with clear upside. Buxton, who was coming off his best season in years, was limited to just 93 games because of a hip injury that ultimately required surgery. He’ll be 33 years old next season, with just one season over 105 games played since 2017 and coming off major hip surgery. A bit on him inside the top 80 is a huge risk, but we also know Buxton can produce fantasy value in 80-100 games. Suzuki is less of an injury risk but more of a team context risk since we have no idea where he’ll be playing next year. Perhaps it could provide a boost to his home run potential. Maybe the team context will limit his counting stats. We won’t know that for a while.
Two more starting pitchers also go here in Max Fried (SP21) and Payton Tolle (SP22), and, spoiler alert, one of them looks like a huge steal. When my starting pitching rankings come out later this week, I will have Tolle in my top 10 starting pitchers. He’ll be slotted right ahead of a tier of aces who have a history of injury (Crochet, Sale, deGrom, Wheeler), so maybe you want to call Tolle a top 15 starter if you’d take all of those injury risks over him. Still, getting a potential top 15 starting pitcher with pick 82 is tremendous. In case you think top-15 is rich for Tolle, he finished as the SP25 this season, and that was while recording just nine wins in 26 starts. He had a 3.03 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, and 28.4% strikeout rate and will be just 24 years old next season. As his breaking balls continue to develop, his performance should only improve.
| Round 8 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 85 | Jorge Montanez | Zack Gelof | 2B/OF | OAK |
| 86 | Justin Mason | Chase DeLauter | OF | CLE |
| 87 | James Schiano | Aroldis Chapman | RP | BOS |
| 88 | Frank Ammirante | Hunter Brown | SP | HOU |
| 89 | Dave Shovein | Freddie Freeman | 1B | LAD |
| 90 | Matthew Pouliot | Louis Varland | RP | TOR |
| 91 | Rivers McCown | Mason Montgomery | RP | PIT |
| 92 | Scott Pianowski | Mookie Betts | SS | LAD |
| 93 | D.J. Short | Tyler Soderstrom | 1B/OF | OAK |
| 94 | Frank Stampfl | Bryan Baker | RP | TB |
| 95 | George Bissell | Grant Taylor | RP | CHW |
| 96 | Roto Pat | JJ Wetherholt | SS | STL |
After Josh Hader went off the board in the last round as RP5, we got a run on closers here in the eighth round with Aroldis Chapman (RP6), Louis Varland (RP7), Mason Montgomery (RP8), Bryan Baker (RP9), and Grant Taylor (RP10). Hader and Chapman are the two established names among the group and make clear sense here, and Baker tied for the MLB lead in saves this season and will return for the potential World Series champion Rays. I’d say that makes him a solid top-ten closer. The other three are all bets on upside, and all bets that make sense. Varland was electric as a closer for the Blue Jays this season and finished as RP3 on the year. Taylor and Montgomery weren’t even full-time closers, and they finished as RP6 and RP7, respectively, due to their high innings totals and strikeout rates. The potential issue for both Taylor and Montgomery is that we have no idea if they will be used as traditional closers. Montgomery feels like the better bet since he had 18 saves this season, but it also took the Pirates a while to turn the role over to him, and they may prefer him in the “fireman” role in the same way the White Sox seem to prefer Taylor. That said, both of them are dominant relief arms.
Three young hitters also went in this round with Zack Gelof, Chase DeLauter, and JJ Wetherholt. Wetherholt as a top 100 pick after his rookie season makes sense, and DeLauter also clearly has the profile of a top 10 pick. His issue has been, and always will be, health risk. Yet, he did manage to play 133 games this season, hitting .287/.363/.457 with 16 home runs and 11 steals. The hard-hit rates suggest that more power could be coming if he can lift the ball a bit more consistently.
Jorge’s pick of Gelof is also a bet that the 26-year-old really did reinvent himself this season, when he hit .256/.322/.475 with 22 home runs and 16 steals in 111 games. Gelof chased less outside of the zone, took a more patient approach overall, made more contact than he ever has, and was less pull-happy than he had been previously. All of that seems to suggest very real growth. Can the growth hold? That will be the big question you have to ask yourself if you draft him in the top 85 picks next season.
We also saw Hunter Brown go off the board here as SP23. If you had told people in March that you’d get Hunter Brown near the end of the eighth round, it would have seemed like a major coup. However, the Astros ace returned from a shoulder injury this season and never looked like himself. Is the injury still lingering, or was 2025 a bit of a fluke? Remember that he had a 3.49 ERA, 1.27 WHIP, and 25% strikeout rate in 2024. There was a major jump forward in 2025, but much of that was in the first half of the season. Even though his ratios remained strong after the All-Star break in 2025, his strikeout rate fell to 24%. So maybe Brown is more of a low 3.00-ERA pitcher who will post a 26% strikeout rate. That’s not a bad profile, but it’s not a top 15 arm. Then you have the health questions to factor in as well, so his slide here makes a bit of sense to me.

item.content:encoded:
Mets should pursue one of two Chicago Cubs stars, even with Juan Soto and Carson Benge originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Given how average the New York Mets were offensively a season ago, it feels safe to say something has to give regarding adding a player or two this offseason.
The Mets seem set in the outfield right now, led by Juan Soto, A.J. Ewing, and Carson Benge, but they could also decide to ignore certain positions and focus on fielding the best possible lineup.
In that scenario, targeting a couple of offensive players this offseason could be a wise move. Two guys in particular who fit that bill are Seiya Suzuki and Ian Happ. Bleacher Report recently suggested both could interest the Mets, even with the existing outfield looking set.
"The Mets appear to have their present and future outfield in place with Juan Soto and 2026 rookies Carson Benge and A.J. Ewing, but designated hitter is a potential area to upgrade. The DH spot produced a .213/.310/.378 line this past season, and with their limitless budget, a run at signing Suzuki to fill that hole is not out of the question," Joel Reuter wrote.
Soto is one of the best players in baseball, Benge has a real chance to be a superstar, and Ewing looks like a guy the Mets can count on for a long time.
All three of those guys will be in the lineup every day, or should be, but that doesn't mean bringing in a guy like Suzuki or Happ has to change that.
The only question for the Mets is whether they're willing to spend money on those guys, since they could be expensive given the lack of talent.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Why Red Sox Could Pursue Japan Triple-Crown Winner Seeking Move To MLB This Offseason

item.content:encoded:
Why Red Sox Could Pursue Japan Triple-Crown Winner Seeking Move To MLB This Offseason originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
If there's one thing the Red Sox need to add to their lineup this offseason, it's power.
Boston ranked 26th among all MLB teams — and third-to-last among squads that made the postseason — in home runs this past season, hitting 163 as a unit with Willson Contreras' 27 leading the way. Against the Yankees in the AL Wild Card series, the Red Sox had just four extra-base hits over two games.
There are a number of names who could be available, whether through free agency or via trade, that Craig Breslow could pursue. One of them is a potential boom-or-bust candidate: Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato, who is seeking a move to MLB through the posting system.
Here's what to know about Sato, a triple-crown winner in Japan's Central League, and why he could be a fit in Boston.
MORE: Inside Payton Tolle's breakout 2026 season
Will Teruaki Sato Be Posted to MLB?
Sato, who plays for the Hanshin Tigers of the Central League in Japan, has been seeking a move to MLB this offseason. As of Monday, his Tigers squad made it official, announcing that Sato would be posted to MLB teams this offseason, per MLB Trade Rumors.
He won the Triple Crown in the Central League, also claiming MVP honors, making him a fascinating potential addition for an MLB franchise this offseason. "At least five" teams have already shown interest in Sato, per MLB Trade Rumors, and in a weaker offensive free-agent class, he could be one of the top available bats.
Sato, 27, is still relatively young and can play third base or right field. It's his bat, however, that would be an asset, as he's been one of the best hitters in Nippon Professional Baseball over the last two seasons. In 2026, he had a .306/.383/.609 slash line with 39 homers and 106 RBI, winning the Triple Crown.
I see a lot of varying data points from Teruaki Sato. Here is his OFFICIAL NPB-licensed data: 117.0 MaxEV 93.3 Avg. EV (Sat over 94 much of 26’) 74.6 MPH Avg. Bat Speed ⚡️ 55.3% Hard-Hit% 18.4% Barrel% 35.7% Chase% 29.5 ft/s Max Sprint Speed https://t.co/rAxDwIiKSs
— LouisAnalysis (@LouisAnalysis) October 20, 2026
Sato wouldn't officially be posted "until some time after the NPB season is over," per MLB Trade Rumors. He would have 45 days to sign with an MLB team after being posted, a timeline that could be impacted by a potential lockout — if he didn't have a contract by Dec. 1, his timeline would pick up where it left off after a lockout ends. If Sato didn't have a contract by the end of the 45-day period, he would return to the Central League in 2027.
After also playing for Japan in the 2026 World Baseball Classic, Sato could join the likes of Shohei Ohtani, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Seiya Suzuki, Shota Imanga, Roki Sasaki, Munetaka Murakami, Kazuma Okamoto and more Japanese stars to join MLB in recent years.
Why Red Sox Could Be A Fit for Teruaki Sato
It's no guarantee that Sato will decide to join MLB, but it appears more likely than not that he'll land a free-agent deal this offseason, especially considering the thin market for bats. Considering Boston has a clear need for a slugger, it wouldn't be surprising to see Breslow kick the tires on adding Sato.
Under Breslow, the Red Sox have proven willing to pursue top Japan talent, signing Masataka Yoshida to a five-year deal in 2023. That deal has not panned out as anticipated, with Yoshida hitting 34 home runs over four seasons, but perhaps Breslow views Sato differently as a final piece to Boston's lineup, needing some power.
In a best-case scenario, Murakami is an example for teams to be encouraged about when considering Sato, a high-strikeout slugger from Japan coming to MLB. After signing with the White Sox last offseason, Murakami hit 35 home runs on a resurgent Chicago team that returned to the postseason, although he also hit .207 with 196 strikeouts.
With Jarren Duran facing an uncertain future in Boston, it wouldn't be surprising to see the Red Sox pursue a slugger — either at DH or in the outfield — to pair with Ceddanne Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu and Roman Anthony. Sato would also be capable of playing third base, where Curtis Mead is currently projected to start in 2027.
He may not be a seamless fit, and the strikeout issues could be a red flag, but there's reason to believe Sato could succeed in Boston. At the very least, he's one of few power bats who could be available, something the Red Sox need.

item.title: [Heavy.com] Red Sox’s Seiya Suzuki Fit Comes With a Surprising Roster Twist
item.dc:creator: Alvin Garcia
item.description: The Boston Red Sox could add more than one power bat by putting Seiya Suzuki on their offseason shopping list. They could also make their lineup more flexible, provided they settle the playing-time questions before committing. Boston.com’s Conor Ryan identified Suzuki as a potential fit earlier this month. The argument is worth revisiting as the free-agent market approaches, though it doesn’t mean Boston has opened negotiations. Suzuki finished 2026 with a .270/.368/.473 slash line and 26 home r
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox could add more than one power bat by putting Seiya Suzuki on their offseason shopping list.
They could also make their lineup more flexible, provided they settle the playing-time questions before committing.
Boston.com’s Conor Ryan identified Suzuki as a potential fit earlier this month. The argument is worth revisiting as the free-agent market approaches, though it doesn’t mean Boston has opened negotiations.
Suzuki finished 2026 with a .270/.368/.473 slash line and 26 home runs, according to Baseball Savant. Those numbers supply the obvious attraction. His ability to work in an outfield and designated hitter rotation creates the more interesting question for Boston.
Suzuki Could Add More Than Right-Handed Power
FanGraphs’ playing-time record lists 111 games in right field and 30 at designated hitter this season. Boston would therefore be evaluating someone with recent experience in both roles.
That flexibility could matter when building a schedule around Roman Anthony. If the Red Sox want Anthony to play DH occasionally, an acquisition who can play the outfield offers more options than a hitter restricted to one lineup spot.
It wouldn’t create extra plate appearances on its own. Boston would still have to account for Wilyer Abreu and the rest of its outfield, and any arrangement would depend on how the roster changes.
The point is to evaluate Suzuki as part of a full alignment. A lineup that gets stronger on days Anthony needs a different assignment has value beyond one player’s home run total.
That is also why an apparent outfield surplus can be misleading. A group can look crowded on paper while still leaving the manager short of suitable choices when an injury or a planned rest day changes the preferred starting lineup.
That benefit would depend on defensive performance, health, and a role Suzuki would actually accept.
The Best Fit Still Needs a Realistic Price
Seiya Suzuki #27 of the Chicago Cubs warms up before game two of the National League Wild Card Series against the San Diego Padres at Petco Park on September 30, 2026 in San Diego, California. (Photo by Orlando Ramirez/Getty Images)
There are reasons to proceed carefully.
Suzuki is 32, so contract length would matter. Boston would need to consider how the proposed arrangement might change if more of his future playing time shifts toward designated hitter.
A flexible player can become a less flexible investment if the contract outlasts the skills that made the original fit attractive. That possibility belongs in the evaluation alongside his offensive production.
The Red Sox should also avoid assuming Fenway Park would automatically produce a career season. A favorable theoretical fit still has to survive the opposing pitchers, daily workload, and normal variation of a long schedule.
A signing would work best if it improved Boston’s choices throughout the week, rather than forcing the same difficult compromise into every game.
Suzuki deserves consideration because Boston can imagine a specific job for him beyond simply adding a recognizable name. The decision should follow a clear plan: identify the available at-bats, establish a realistic defensive workload, and decide what that combined role is worth before entering a bidding contest.

item.title: [CubsHQ] Randy Arozarena emerges as intriguing outfield option
item.dc:creator: Dustin Riese
item.description: Sooner or later, the Chicago Cubs will have to address the many question marks heading into the offseason, with one of the biggest concerns surrounding their outfield. With both Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki potentially heading to the open market, the Cubs could suddenly find themselves down two corner outfielders. If that happens, they will need to do whatever it takes to fill those spots with reliable players. The Cubs' goal will be to retain at least one of those two players, but given how active
item.content:encoded:
Sooner or later, the Chicago Cubs will have to address the many question marks heading into the offseason, with one of the biggest concerns surrounding their outfield.
With both Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki potentially heading to the open market, the Cubs could suddenly find themselves down two corner outfielders. If that happens, they will need to do whatever it takes to fill those spots with reliable players.
The Cubs' goal will be to retain at least one of those two players, but given how active the free-agent market could be, that may not be as easy as it seems. If the Cubs can't bring one of them back, don't be surprised if they look elsewhere. Randy Arozarena could be an option in left field and, at the very least, could help fill one of those two spots.
Despite being 32, Arozarena still has plenty left in the tank. Given the way he plays the game, especially defensively, adding that kind of energy alongside Pete Crow-Armstrong could be a great fit. Comparable to Suzuki in terms of age and offensive production, Arozarena is coming off an impressive season and has established himself as an above-average hitter since becoming an everyday player with the Tampa Bay Rays.
This past season proves it: Arozarena slashed .281/.381/.484 with a 151 wRC+. He added 26 home runs while posting a 10% walk rate and a strikeout rate just above 20%. Those numbers reflect a disciplined approach at the plate and help explain why he remains a productive offensive player.
As impressive as his production has been, concerns about Arozarena are growing. His overall bat speed and barrel rate are trending downward, raising questions about whether he can sustain his recent success. Still, this year's free-agent class offers few proven, productive bats, making a player with Arozarena's offensive capabilities hard to overlook.
Another major concern is his defensive value, as he continues to grade out near the bottom of the league. For a team that prides itself on defense and making plays for its pitchers, would adding a below-average defender in left field to replace a potential Gold Glove-caliber outfielder really make sense?
Maybe not. Still, the Cubs need to find ways to improve their roster, and Arozarena could offer an offensive upgrade in left field. What he may lack defensively, he could make up for with his postseason experience. On the biggest stage, Arozarena has built a reputation as one of baseball's most dangerous postseason performers.
Known for delivering in big moments, Arozarena could bring a spark to a Cubs team that has struggled to create memorable postseason moments in recent years. That kind of energy and experience could provide something the franchise hasn't enjoyed consistently since its 2016 championship run.
Another aspect of Arozarena's game that is sometimes overlooked is his ability on the basepaths. He added 23 stolen bases to his 26 home runs and impressive offensive numbers, giving him another dimension that could benefit the Cubs.
His speed would pair nicely with what Crow-Armstrong brings to the table, potentially giving the Cubs another base-stealing threat near the top of their lineup. With career highs in batting average, on-base percentage, and slugging percentage, Arozarena is coming off one of the best offensive seasons of his career.
Producing at that level at this stage of his career is somewhat surprising, but it also raises an important question: Can he do it again?
Some players take longer to find their footing in the big leagues, and Arozarena's career has followed a somewhat unconventional path. He didn't receive a regular, everyday opportunity until he broke through with Tampa Bay. Since then, his production has had its ups and downs, including during his time with the Seattle Mariners.
Even so, Arozarena has shown that he can be a productive offensive player, and his recent success in Seattle has only added to the intrigue surrounding his free agency. The question now is whether the player we saw this past season is the version of Arozarena fans can expect going forward or whether his production will regress toward his previous levels.
Arozarena is expected to command a lucrative contract, potentially worth at least $100 million, which could put him outside the Cubs' price range. However, given the team's potential outfield needs, don't be surprised if Chicago makes a serious run at him in free agency.

item.content:encoded:
退団は不可避なのか…。今季限りでカブスとの５年契約が満了となる鈴木誠也外野手（３２）の去就が毎日のように米メディアでクローズアップされている。
１９日（日本時間２０日）には、今オフＦＡとなる選手に今季の所属球団が提示できる１年契約「クオリファイング・オファー（ＱＯ）」の規定額が「２３１５万ドル（約３６億円）」になったと伝えられた。攻守にわたる活躍でカブスの主軸となっている鈴木もＱＯを提示される可能性が十分あるが、残留には早くも絶望感が漂っている。
球団の専門メディア「ＣＵＢＢＩＥＳ ＣＲＩＢ」は「昨年、ＦＡ選手の１人がこのオファーを受け入れたが、鈴木の場合はそうならない可能性が高い」と断じた。というのも、鈴木は４年連続で２０本塁打以上と安定した長打力を発揮するだけでなく、ゴールドグラブ賞では右翼手部門の最終候補にも残っている。
同メディアはブルージェイズをはじめ、マリナーズやヤンキースなどが獲得に乗り出すとみられることを伝えた上で「ＱＯの有無にかかわらず、入札合戦が繰り広げられる可能性が高い。それがカブスが再びチームに迎え入れられない主な理由」と諦めモードだ。
鈴木の新契約は１億ドル（約１５８億円）規模になるとも試算されている。カブスも資金注入に本腰を入れれば引き留められる可能性もあるが、同メディアは悲観的だ。
「確かに今オフシーズンに１億ドル以上の年俸負担が軽減されるカブスには、鈴木の争奪戦でトップに立つだけの資金力がある。しかし、資金の大部分が投手陣の補強に充てられる見込みで、カブスが鈴木の争奪戦に勝つことを事実上不可能にしている」
鈴木を残したくてもすべてを残留費用に回すわけにもいかない。「ＱＯを提示する可能性はあるが、結末は既定路線」と流出は避けられないとみられている。

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Projecting Tarik Skubal's Historic Contract, Bo Bichette Payday, More MLB Free Agency
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown
item.description: When the 2026 Major League Baseball season officially comes to an end, the next big thing to watch is going to be what happens with two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal. Skubal is the biggest free agent prize of the year, without a doubt. He follows in the footsteps of guys like Shohei Ohtani, Juan Soto and Kyle Tucker, who were the biggest free agents of the year over the last three years. This year, it's time for Skubal to cash in. Beyond Skubal, the biggest free agents of the offseason
item.content:encoded:
When the 2026 Major League Baseball season officially comes to an end, the next big thing to watch is going to be what happens with two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal.
Skubal is the biggest free agent prize of the year, without a doubt. He follows in the footsteps of guys like Shohei Ohtani, Juan Soto and Kyle Tucker, who were the biggest free agents of the year over the last three years. This year, it's time for Skubal to cash in.
Beyond Skubal, the biggest free agents of the offseason are Randy Arozarena, Seiya Suzuki, Robbie Ray, Shota Imanaga and potentially Bo Bichette. Bichette has an opt-out in his deal with the New York Mets. It's going to be a fun few months across the league. Let's try our hand at projecting what it could cost to sign these top names.
Tarik Skubal — Starting Pitcher
Skubal's stint in free agency is going to be fascinating. On one hand, you have the hurler who has been the most dominant starter in baseball over the last three years, at least. On the other hand, Skubal is heading to free agency at 29 years old and after undergoing elbow surgery earlier in the season.
Skubal is the best player heading to the open market and he will get paid well. He even could get paid historically well. ESPN's Jeff Passan shared in a column that if there is no salary cap, he could double the $245 million deal Stephen Strasburg got from the Washington Nationals, at most. Arguably, that is far too high. Yoshinobu Yamamoto has the largest contract for a starter in big league history at $325 million over 12 years, but he got that at 25 years old. Gerrit Cole is a closer equivalent. He got his nine-year, $324 million deal at 29 years old. Skubal should come in much closer to that from a years perspective. But could very well top Yamamoto's overall value.
Projection: 8-years, $335 million ($41.8 AAV).
Randy Arozarena — Outfielder
Arozarena is a three-time All-Star, including each of the last two years, and is coming off a 5.7 WAR season. He picked a good time to have one of the best seasons of his career. Arozarena is the best non-Bichette bat heading to the open market, which should do wonders for his value.
Projection: 5-years, $120 million
Seiya Suzuki — Outfielder
Suzuki is the second-best non-Bichette offensive player heading to the open market. He's coming off a season in which he hit 26 home runs, drove in 86 runs and logged 31 doubles in 143 games played. He'll be 32 years old when the 2027 season begins. He should do quite well this winter.
Projection: 4-years, $90 million
Robbie Ray — Starting Pitcher
Ray may be 35 years old, but he can still get it down. He had a 3.59 ERA in 31 total appearances in 2026, including 30 starts, with the San Francisco Giants and the San Diego Padres. He was an All-Star in 2025. Ray won't turn 36 years old until October, 2027. He should get one more multi-year deal this offseason.
Projection: 3-years, $55 million
Shota Imanaga — Starting Pitcher
Imanaga is just 33 years old and hasn't had more than a 3.77 season ERA in his three-year big league career. He's younger than Ray and has been arguably better over the last three seasons. He should do even better in free agency.
Projection: 3-years, $64 million
Bo Bichette — Infielder
Bichette is going to be among the most intriguing players to follow over the next few weeks. Skubal is clearly the best free agent heading to the open market. If Bichette opts out, he'll be the second-best. Bichette is owed $42 million from the Mets, if he sticks around in 2027. Then, he has a $42 million player option for 2028.
It's hard to believe, but Bichette is still just 28 years old. If he were to enter the open market again, there should be a massive deal with his name on it.
Projection: 6-Years, $200 million
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick also received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Fastball On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Bo Bichette’s Opt-Out Looms Over a Thin Third Base Market
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown
item.description: The upcoming free agent market is going to be thin, to say the least. Right now, the top offensive weapons scheduled to head to the open market are outfielders Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki. item.content:encoded:
The upcoming free agent market is going to be thin, to say the least.
Right now, the top offensive weapons scheduled to head to the open market are outfielders Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki. Arozarena smacked 26 home runs and drove in 79 runs in 54 games for the Seattle Mariners in 2026. Suzuki hit 26 home runs and drove in 86 runs for the Chicago Cubs in 143 games played. Outside of these two, the top offensive bats who are pending free agents are George Springer, Gleyber Torres, Trent Grisham, Ian Happ, Eugenio Suarez, Jonathan India, among others. There's a clear difference between Arozarena and Suzuki, and the rest of the top bats heading to the open market.
One guy who could throw a wrench into free agency is infielder Bo Bichette. The two-time All-Star has an opt-out to consider this offseason. If he doesn't use it, he'll make $42 million in 2027. If he does use it, all of a sudden he becomes the most intriguing offensive free agent. Plus, it helps that the third base market is going to be very thin.
What Should Bo Bichette Do?
Bichette didn't have a great 2026 season. He slashed .260/.312/.390 with 18 home runs and 78 RBIs in 160 games played. But he is still just 28 years old. He'll turn 29 years old before the 2027 season begins. Both Arozarena and Suzuki will be 32 years old by the time the 2027 season starts. Bichette is roughly four years younger.
When it comes to third base specifically, Suarez technically has a mutual option, but those are rarely ever picked up. Suarez is now 35 years old and batted .212 in 2026. He has significant pop, but didn't make contact and isn't great defensively at this point. Alec Bohm will be a free agent. He's 30 years old and has question marks himself. After Bichette, Suarez and Bohm, the next best options will be guys like Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Yoan Moncada and Jeimer Candelario.
If Bichette becomes available, he is head and shoulders above the rest of the potential third base free agent options. Plus, he can play other spots in the infield as well. Bichette was the Toronto Blue Jays' shortstop for years and he can play second base as well.
At the end of the day, Bichette has a decision to make. If he opts out, he should be in line for an even bigger multi-year deal.

item.content:encoded:
カブス・鈴木誠也外野手（３２）の市場価値が高騰中だ。今季限りで５年契約が満了となり、来季の所属球団がどこになるのか米メディアを連日にぎわせている。
今季は１４３試合に出場して打率２割７分、２６本塁打、８６打点、ＯＰＳ０・８４１をマークし、守備力の向上も評価されて右翼手部門でゴールドグラブ賞の最終候補にも残った。攻守にわたる安定した活躍で外野手としてＦＡ市場の目玉の一人となっている。
当然、カブスとしては来季も必要な戦力。球団の専門メディア「ＣＵＢＢＩＥＳ ＣＲＩＢ」は１７日（日本時間１８日）に「イアン・ハップと鈴木という主力野手の退団に直面している。１人は新たな契約で呼び戻す方法を探す必要がある」と流出阻止を唱えた。
鈴木の契約は５年総額８５００万ドル（約１３５億円＝当時）で年平均１７００万ドル（約２７億円）だった。同メディアはプロスポーツ選手の契約などをデータ化する米サイト「ｓｐｏｔｒａｃ」がはじき出した「４年総額９０００万ドル（約１４２億円）」「平均年俸２２５０万ドル（約５６億２０００万円）」の予想価格をもとに「カブスは鈴木を呼び戻すためにあらゆる手を尽くすべきだ」と資金の捻出を迫った。
ところが、同日のうちに「ｓｐｏｔｒａｃ」が示した鈴木の〝適正価格〟は「４年総額１億０９９６万ドル（約１７３億８０００万円）」まで上昇。一気に２０００万ドル（約３２億円）近くも跳ね上がった格好だ。
鈴木にとっては選手としてそれだけ高い評価を得ている証しでもあるが、価格が高騰するほど残留の可能性が低くなっていくことも考えられる。波乱含みのオフとなりそうだ。

item.title: [FanSided] Projecting MLB free agency deals for Tarik Skubal and baseball's biggest stars
item.dc:creator: Christopher Kline

item.content:encoded:
MLB free agency takes on a new urgency this winter with a Dec. 1 lockout on the horizon. That could change how teams operate — and, eventually, how much money teams are allowed to spend, or even forced to spend. There are a ton of unknown variables at this point.
What we do know (for the most part) are which stars will be available to sign when the market does open up. From Los Angeles Dodgers ace Tarik Skubal to top Japanese free agent Teruaki Sato, here are the 10 best free agents (according to FanSided's Robert Murray) with projected contracts and destinations.
LHP Tarik Skubal
Projected deal: 9 years, $378 million ($42 million AAV) with New York Mets
Regardless of how CBA negotiations shake out, Tarik Skubal's long-rumored $400 million price tag may ultimately prove to be an overestimation. There's a reason no pitcher has ever received such a paycheck, Shohei Ohtani notwithstanding. Still, Skubal should become the highest-paid pitcher in MLB history. His durability, both in-game and season-long, combined with razor-sharp stuff in the prime of his career, should give teams the confidence to invest in Skubal over an extended period.
The Dodgers are the natural landing spot after acquiring him at the trade deadline, but the Mets are baseball's richest team and there's mounting pressure for New York to start competing, in a serious way, with Juan Soto and Francisco Lindor. Skubal is the ultimate floor-raiser in a rotation, and he'd form a mean one-two punch with breakout ace Nolan McLean.
OF Seiya Suzuki
Projected deal: 4 years, $100 million ($25 million AAV) with Toronto Blue Jays
Seiya Suzuki is probably the best bat available in free agency. The 32-year-old outfielder has been a model of consistency for the Cubs, with at least 20 home runs and an .800-plus OPS in three straight seasons. He's a plus defender in right field, too, where he posted career-best metrics in 2026. Suzuki has a rocket-like arm and consistently holds runners from the back corner.
Plenty of teams will take an interest in Suzuki's right-handed power profile; he draws walks and operates with sage discipline in the batter's box, despite occasionally elevated strikeout numbers. In the end, Toronto represents the most logical intersection of need and financial firepower to outbid the field.
OF Randy Arozarena
Projected deal: 5 years, $110 million ($22 million AAV) with Philadelphia Phillies
Randy Arozarena set new career highs in average (.281), OPS (.865) and home runs (26) in his walk year, emerging as one of the few bright spots on an otherwise disappointing Mariners team. He's more adequate than exceptional with his glove, but Arozarena provides middle-order power and he's a great personality hire.
The Phillies need Arozarena's bat and competitive fire in equal measure, plus he can help to safely return Bryce Harper to first base next season. Philadelphia desperately needs a right-handed slugger behind Harper in the lineup; the ability to finally add some stability to the outfield depth chart, as opposed to a 2026 rewind of the Adolis García or Max Kepler situations, should greatly appeal to a desperate Dave Dombrowski.
3B Teruaki Sato
Projected deal: 3 years, $75 million ($25 million AAV) with New York Yankees
Teruaki Sato is the most accomplished international free agent hoping to come Stateside this offseason. An MVP candidate in Japan's NPB, Sato hit .306 this year with 39 home runs and a .991 OPS. There are swing-and-miss and defense concerns, not dissimilar to the vague uncertainties that tanked Munetaka Murakami's stock last winter. Murakami ended up on a two-year deal with the White Sox, which he immediately outperformed.
Sato's left-handed power and upside at 27 years old could mean his market flourishes. But, given the baked-in gambles that come with signing an international free agent, he could end up getting lowballed, much like Murakami. A three-year, $75 million contract gives Sato a nice payday upfront while still hedging against potential struggles with a short-term framework. The Yankees need an infield slugger and have the money to roll the dice, so to speak, on Sato's immense talent.
LHP Trevor Rogers
Projected deal: 3 years, $60 million ($20 million) with Baltimore Orioles
Trevor Rogers has dealt with his share of injuries and inconsistency over the years, but he's coming off of two strong campaigns in Baltimore — and he's only 28 years old, so there's room left to establish himself as more than a third or fourth starter type. He couldn't recapture the success of 2025, when Rogers returned from injury to post a 1.81 ERA in 18 starts, but his 4.03 ERA last season does not capture the strength of his stuff (3.60 xERA). Moreover, the career-high 30 starts and 169.2 innings pitched was a nice addition to his résumé.
Teams will probably balk at dropping a full bag on Rogers' doorstep, ultimately, which opens the door for a short-term contract (probably with an opt-out clause or two) and a return to Baltimore. The Orioles need pitching badly and there are precious few better options than Rogers floating around the open market. This contract could turn into a total bargain.
RHP Freddy Peralta
Projected deal: 4 years, $84 million ($21 million AAV) with Chicago Cubs
Freddy Peralta's walk year has been a roller coaster of emotions. He bombed in New York after the Mets dealt multiple top-100 prospects to acquire him in an offseason trade. Then, after relocating to Tampa at the trade deadline, Peralta started slow before gradually picking up steam in September. Down the stretch and into the playoffs, he has looked more like the Cy Young candidate we witnessed in Milwaukee last season.
Peralta has not made the strongest case to prospective suitors in 2026, so a one-year, high-AAV deal to "prove it" is on the table. Ultimately, however, the 30-year-old should still be able to coax a substantial multi-year offer out of a desperate contender. His longtime NL Central rivals, the Cubs, are one such desperate contender. Peralta could join with the now-healthy Cade Horton and Justin Steele to revitalize Chicago's World Series hopes for 2027.
C Ryan Jeffers
Projected deal: 4 years, $68 million ($17 million AAV) with Minnesota Twins
The catcher market is tough to project, as there are so few who can hit like Ryan Jeffers. He was excellent in Minnesota this season, with 14 home runs and an .814 OPS in roughly half a season. He's the best catcher on the market, but Jeffers is not exactly lauded for his defense nor his game management behind the plate. He is not without injury concerns either, while even the best catchers end up in a timeshare eventually (especially when, like Jeffers, their glovework can be problematic).
Since there is such an absence of reliable hitters at the catcher position, Jeffers should be able to land a solid multi-year deal in the middle of his prime. A return to the Twins should not be discounted, even with Eduardo Tait and Vahn Lackey coming up through the Minors on accelerated timelines. Minnesota made a conscious decision not to trade him at the deadline, after all. The Twins would probably like to compete next season.
RHP Michael King
Projected deal: five years, $120 million ($24 million AAV) with San Diego Padres
Michael King returned to San Diego last winter on a backloaded three-year deal with opt outs. After an excellent showing in the playoffs, he will probably axe the remaining two years and $66 million on that contract in hopes of securing more guaranteed money this winter. King is not the sexiest name on the pitching market by any stretch, but he has made himself into a dependable workhorse with October equity.
The Padres clearly love King and new ownership, with their stated intention to build a contender, will probably consent to a reworked contract. San Diego has a paper-thin rotation as is. Losing King without a viable alternative in place could be disastrous, as the Padres don't have the trade ammo to compensate for a free agency exodus.
2B Brandon Lowe
Projected deal: 3 years, $66 million ($22 million AAV) with Pittsburgh Pirates
Brandon Lowe arrived in Pittsburgh via offseason trade and immediately became the most bankable presence in their lineup, with 35 home runs, 96 RBI and an .824 OPS. The 32-year-old can get in trouble with swing-and-miss, but he's a slugging outlier at second base. Moreover, Lowe quietly posted some of the best defensive metrics in MLB last season after struggling for years on the defensive end. It's fair to be skeptical about Lowe's ability to sustain this elite defense into his mid-30s, but he did everything he could to maximize his value as a free agent.
To that point, it's hard to imagine the Pirates letting Lowe walk without a fight. Pittsburgh threw more money around last offseason, with the front office clearly committed to changing their postseason fortunes. It did not come together in 2026, but Pittsburgh has a dangerous lineup and a very talented pitching staff. There's potential for a breakthrough in 2027, especially if Lowe sticks around.
LHP Adrián Morejón
Projected deal: 4 years, $68 million ($17 million AAV) with Toronto Blue Jays
Adrián Morejón's mystery-shrouded absence in San Diego's NLDS loss to Milwaukee was a tough pill to swallow, but once again, the Padres end the season feeling like the second-best team in the National League. They were able to at least put a scare into the Brewers where even the Dodgers could not. Part of the reason for San Diego's success this season, despite dramatic fluctuations from their lineup, was an elite bullpen. Morejón was only the setup man to Mason Miller, but the 27-year-old southpaw is still among the best relievers in baseball.
Over the past three seasons, Morejón has a 2.58 ERA with 248 strikeouts in 223.1 innings. It's hard to find a more steadfast high-leverage arm, especially one as young as Morejón. He could get some real length on his contract in a reliever-needy marketplace. The Blue Jays figure to be as aggressive as any team this offseason; Morejón setting up Louis Varland, with Tyler Rogers and Spencer Miles to cover other late-inning spots, is a tantalizing proposition.
